summary: Focused technical review of Redwood Private deployment for Borealis Retail. Covered VPC zoning, ingress patterns, egress gateway options, firewall rules, KMS/HSM integration, RBAC/SSO mapping, and audit log delivery to SIEM. Agreed to run a controlled throughput test to validate egress gateway performance and to exchange a concrete list of audit fields and retention windows.
topics: Ingress via ALB vs private ingress proxy
Egress gateway and outbound firewall policies
Audit logs to SIEM (Splunk/Datadog) and retention
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-27 07:00 PT | Duration: 58m | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Elaine Cho (Solutions), Rajesh Nair (CTO - Borealis), Priya Rao (Head Infra), Tommy Li (Security Architect), Ava Moreno (Compliance)

00:00 Speaker 1 (Sofia): Morning everyone, thanks for coming, really appreciate you taking the time, we wanted to run through the Private deployment specifics given your data residency and audit needs.
00:18 Speaker 2 (Rajesh): Yeah thanks, Sofia. We got a few hard constraints: all PII must remain in our Toronto region, we need SOC 2–level audit trails, SSO via Okta, and an HSM-backed key store. Also curious on how egress can be constrained so tokens never leak outbound.
00:40 Speaker 3 (Marco): Great, we can architect that. At a high level Redwood Private runs a control plane we can host in your VPC or via a thin control plane in our cloud with private connectivity — you mentioned you want fully customer-controlled data plane in Toronto?
00:59 Speaker 2 (Rajesh): Correct. No model data should leave customer-managed network unless explicitly allowed.
:08 Speaker 4 (Priya): Quick clarification: when you say control plane in our VPC, do you mean we host all the services or just the orchestration? We want minimal surface in public cloud.
01:22 Speaker 3 (Marco): We recommend a split: customer-owned model-serving nodes and a private control plane endpoint. For strictest isolation, everything (control plane, scheduler, and runtime) can be deployed on-prem or in your VPC. That gives you full egress control.
01:38 Speaker 5 (Tommy): Ok, then how does egress work? We need to ensure outbound to vendor update endpoints or telemetry is either disabled or routed via an approved egress gateway.
01:49 Speaker 3 (Marco): Right. Two patterns: 1) Egress-deny-by-default: restrict all outbound; explicitly allow only approved destinations via an egress NAT/proxy. 2) Egress-proxy with TLS inspection: route all outbound through a customer-managed gateway that performs allowlisting. For the second, we support mTLS between the runtime and the gateway; Redwood can present client certs if you want mutual TLS.
02:15 Speaker 1 (Sofia): And to be explicit about telemetry: we can disable outbound telemetry entirely and instead stream metrics/logs to your SIEM. That avoids any external telemetry endpoints.
02:28 Speaker 2 (Rajesh): Ava, from compliance perspective, what's needed in the logs?
02:33 Speaker 6 (Ava): We need identity bind (who invoked), request metadata (model id, prompt hash), token counts, timestamps, success/failure, and redaction markers so raw PII is not stored in long-term logs. Retention needs to be 7 years for certain audits, but we can tier to shorter retention for non-audit material.
02:53 Speaker 3 (Marco): For log delivery we support syslog, Fluentd/Fluent Bit, and direct ingestion into Splunk/Datadog/CloudWatch. We can ship signed, append-only logs, and you can mount an encrypted S3 bucket (in your region) as long-term archive.
03:10 Speaker 5 (Tommy): On encryption — KMS integration — does Redwood require any key material to leave our HSM? We want to keep key custody in our HSM.
03:21 Speaker 3 (Marco): No, you can bring-your-own-key and keep keys in your HSM. Redwood supports Envelope encryption model: data keys generated in HSM, data encrypted at the runtime with those data keys; only encrypted DEKs (data encryption keys) travel to Redwood services, and they are decryptable only by the HSM. We also support automated rotation and audit logs for key usage.
03:42 Speaker 4 (Priya): How about local KV cache and its persistence? Are caches encrypted at rest?
03:48 Speaker 3 (Marco): Yes, KV caches and any disk (EBS or local NVMe) are encrypted with the data keys. For on-prem you can enforce host-level full disk encryption; for cloud you can rely on provider encryption plus your KMS wrapping.
04:00 Speaker 1 (Sofia): Quick note — we have customers who require no internet egress at all; in that mode all model downloads are staged via airgap tooling and images are scanned and imported into your local registry. We can go fully offline.
04:16 Speaker 2 (Rajesh): Probably not fully airgapped for us but good to know. Our main worry is low latency inference and ensuring the egress proxy doesn't add more than, like, 8–12ms tail latencies.
04:29 Speaker 3 (Marco): That's fair — egress gateway can be colocated and lightweight. Our recommended pattern is a dedicated egress pool with continuous batching and local TLS termination; we've seen <10ms added for optimized paths, but we need to validate with your traffic distribution. We'll run a micro-benchmark.
04:50 Speaker 6 (Ava): On RBAC and SSO: mapping application-level roles to Okta groups is essential. Can Redwood honor least-privilege role mapping so engineers cannot call high-privilege endpoints?
05:03 Speaker 3 (Marco): Yes, Redwood supports SAML/Okta SSO and SCIM provisioning to sync groups. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles (viewer, operator, admin). There is also token-level scoping so API tokens can be limited to models, routes, or rates.
05:20 Speaker 2 (Rajesh): What about audit immutability? We need tamper-proof audit trails for SOC 2.
05:26 Speaker 3 (Marco): Two mechanisms: 1) append-only signed logs delivered to your archive (we sign each log chunk with a rotation key and publish the key fingerprints to you), 2) integrate with your existing WORM-compliant storage (S3 object lock) where we write events. You also get chain-of-custody metadata (who exported, who rotated, etc.).
05:48 Speaker 5 (Tommy): Are there any known gotchas with TLS cert rotation or mTLS client cert expiry? We've seen service outages when certs rotate unexpectedly.
05:58 Speaker 3 (Marco): We have a recommended rotation window and overlap (grace period) so new certs are introduced before old ones expire; certs are automatically rotated and we can also integrate with your cert manager (e.g., Vault PKI or cert-manager) so you control issuance. We log rotations as audit events.
06:12 Speaker 1 (Sofia): Great, I'm going to summarise next steps at the end, but first, can we talk about network zoning — how should customers carve subnets for runtime, control plane, and egress?
06:24 Speaker 4 (Priya): Yes, we want concrete subnet sizing recommendations — how many nodes per availability zone and whether to isolate an autoscaling group per model family.
06:35 Speaker 3 (Marco): Typical pattern: three tiers — control plane in private subnet A, model-serving fleet in private subnet B (dedicated per AZ), and egress/ingress proxies in subnet C. Isolate management plane (SSH/jump hosts) to a separate subnet with strict security groups. Autoscaling groups per model family is a good idea if you need different instance types; otherwise you can pack via instance type labels and scheduling.
06:58 Speaker 2 (Rajesh): For ingress, do you recommend an ALB in front or something internal? We do not want public ALBs terminating customer prompts.
07:07 Speaker 3 (Marco): For private-only traffic, we recommend an internal ALB or an NLB with private IPs and then a TLS-terminating proxy inside the VPC. Alternatively, you can use AWS PrivateLink or equivalent provider private endpoints. If you need external apps to call, use a customer-managed API gateway with WAF and allowlisting.
07:29 Speaker 5 (Tommy): On firewall rules — what minimum egress allowlist entries does Redwood need for Private?
07:36 Speaker 3 (Marco): If you're running fully on-prem with no external telemetry, almost none. If you run a thin control plane that contacts Redwood SaaS, it's generally the control-plane endpoints (.redwood.ai) on TLS 443 and a few CDN IP ranges for model packaging. We'll provide an exact list. For certificate revocation or image signing checks we may need to reach our signing endpoints; these can be mirrored to your internal repo.
07:59 Speaker 1 (Sofia): We'll send the canonical allowlist and a template to paste into your firewall as an IaC snippet.
08:06 Speaker 6 (Ava): One more around privacy: masking/redaction at the prompt level — can Redwood redact tokens before logs are persisted?
08:13 Speaker 3 (Marco): Yes, we support pre-log redaction hooks. You can supply regex redaction rules or use a PII detector plugin; redaction happens before writing to the audit stream. We also support a hashed-prompt mode where we store deterministic hashes for matchability without keeping raw content.
08:32 Speaker 2 (Rajesh): That hashed prompt idea sounds good for telemetry while preserving privacy.
08:36 Speaker 5 (Tommy): For compliance audit readiness, will Redwood provide a package of artifacts (control mappings, SOC 2 attestations, configuration screenshots)?
08:45 Speaker 1 (Sofia): Yes, we'll share our compliance pack, SOC 2 report excerpt, and a guide showing the mapping between your controls and Redwood's features. We also have a runbook template for incident response.
08:56 Speaker 4 (Priya): Anything about pbx or secret sprawl — how do we manage API token rotation?
09:01 Speaker 3 (Marco): Tokens can be short-lived and bound to Okta sessions; we recommend ephemeral tokens with a refresh mechanism. We also support token policies limiting access by IP and model. All token actions are audited.
09:12 Speaker 1 (Sofia): Ok, we've hit 55 minutes, let's close with the commitments.
09:16 Speaker 1 (Sofia): Recap: Marco will produce the benchmark script and run a micro-test to validate egress latency; I'll share the Private deployment runbook + network diagram template; Tommy to provide the list of audit fields and retention; and we'll reconvene after test results. Any final questions?
09:33 Speaker 6 (Ava): No, that's good. Thanks.
09:36 Speaker 2 (Rajesh): Thanks everyone, appreciate the thoroughness.
09:40 Speaker 1 (Sofia): Thanks all — we'll follow up in writing.

End of transcript.
